name: OMAD (one meal a day)

image.caption: Ühiskondlikud probleemid ─ kelle omad, kelle lahendada?

lead: OMAD means one meal a day, usually in a one- to two-hour window. It is a form of intermittent fasting used to cut body fat and get a leaner look with one simple rule.

Compressing eating into one window tends to lower total daily intake, which produces a calorie deficit. Broader intermittent fasting research shows modest weight loss, with limited evidence that it outperforms continuous calorie restriction, and no trials specific to OMAD and appearance were found.

paras: People eat a single large meal and fast the rest of the day, drinking only calorie-free drinks. It is sometimes combined with low-carbohydrate eating or fat-loss drugs, and with resistance training to hold muscle.

Short-term hunger, irritability, dizziness and headaches are reported. Health bodies advise against intermittent fasting for pregnant women, children, older adults, underweight people and those with eating disorders.

angle.text: Users eat all daily food in one sitting as a simple way to run a calorie deficit and lean out. It is a form of time-restricted eating, and no trials have tested OMAD specifically for appearance.

lead: OMAD stands for "one meal a day", an eating pattern in which all daily food is consumed in a single sitting, usually within a one- to two-hour window. Wikipedia classifies it as a subtype of time-restricted eating within intermittent fasting.[1]

Looksmaxxing forum users discuss it as a way to cut body fat, sometimes alongside low-carbohydrate eating or fat-loss drugs. Reviews of intermittent fasting report modest weight loss, with limited evidence that it outperforms continuous calorie restriction, and no trials specific to OMAD and facial appearance were found.[1][2]

paras: In time-restricted eating, food is limited to a daily window often of 8 to 12 hours; OMAD narrows this to about one to two hours.[1]

No clinical trials of OMAD specifically were found. Studies of intermittent fasting more broadly report weight loss of about 2.5 to 9.9 percent in most trials, with limited evidence that it matches continuous calorie restriction, and with dropout rates of 2 to 38 percent.[1] A 2026 review discusses impacts, mechanisms and cautions of intermittent fasting across medical and lifestyle domains.[2] Evidence shows no athletic performance benefit, and fasted exercise reduces performance in efforts over 60 minutes.[1]

Short-term effects of intermittent fasting include hunger, irritability, dizziness, nausea, headaches and impaired thinking, usually fading within a month.[1] It is not recommended for pregnant or breastfeeding women, children, older adults, underweight people, or those with or prone to eating disorders.[1]

Users on looksmax.org describe OMAD as easier to sustain than several small meals, with one poster reporting steady energy and manageable hunger on 1,000 to 1,300 kcal while training.[3] Others ask whether OMAD at about 1,500 kcal causes hair loss, with replies suggesting that extreme deficits rather than moderate ones do.[4] Threads also compare OMAD with water fasting for rapid fat loss before a bulk.[5]

lore.intro: OMAD is discussed as a convenient fat-loss method, with questions about hair loss and hormones.[3][4]

claims.claim: OMAD makes dieting easier because hunger is manageable and meals are larger.
OMAD at moderate calories does not cause hair loss, but extreme deficits do.
